en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Ratanavagga 89.
The Training Rule on Sitting Mats.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a sitting mat had been permitted for the monks by the Blessed One.
The group of six monks,
thinking, "A sitting mat has been permitted by the Blessed One," carried around sitting mats of unlimited size.
They hang them from the front and the back of both beds and benches.
Those monks who have few desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and were indignant, saying:
“How can the group-of-six monks wear sitting cloths of unlimited size? … [as before] …
“Is it true, monks, that you carry oversized sitting mats?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you carry oversized sitting cloths?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Furthermore, when a monk is having a sitting mat made, it should be made according to the proper measure.
Herein, this is the measure: two spans long according to the span of the Sugata, and one and a half spans wide.
For one who exceeds that, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was large-bodied.
Having spread out his sitting mat in front of the Blessed One, he sat down, smoothing it all around him.
Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Udāyī, why are you smoothing your sitting mat all over,
as if it were an old hide?”
“Because, venerable sir, the Blessed One has permitted a sitting cloth that is too small for the bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow, bhikkhus, a fringe of ten spans for the sitting cloth.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“When a monk is having a sitting mat made, it should be made according to the proper measure.
Herein, this is the measure: two spans in length, using the span of the Sugata; one and a half spans in width; a fringe of one span.”
For one who exceeds that [measure], it is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
"Seat" (nisīdana) means it is said to include the border.
"By one who has it made" means that whether making it oneself or having it made by another, it should be made according to the proper measure.
Herein, this is the measure: two spans in length, using the span of the Sugata; one and a half spans across; and a fringe of one span.
If, having exceeded that [measure], one makes it oneself or causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the effort.
Upon obtaining [the robe], having cut it down, a confession of an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) must be made.
If one completes what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation.
If one completes what was begun by oneself with the help of others, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one completes what was begun by others with one's own help, there is an offense of expiation.
If one completes what was begun by others with the help of others, there is an offense of expiation.
If one makes it or causes it to be made for another purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one uses what has been obtained when it was made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
He makes it according to the measure;
he makes it less than the measure;
having obtained something made by another that exceeds the measure, he cuts it down and uses it.
If one makes a canopy, or a floor-covering, or a screen-wall, or a mattress,
or a pillow— except for one who is insane or the first offender.
The seventh training rule on sitting mats is finished.
